issues.legal_issue: A writ court may record and give effect to a compromise without requiring strict compliance with the formal requirements for compromises in civil suits.
material_facts: The writ petition was disposed of after counsel for both sides asked the court to record the terms in a government memorandum that had been issued following the Endowments Commissioner’s proposal.
The memorandum set out the proposed terms in writing, and the respondent accepted those terms during the writ proceedings.
The appellants did not contend that their counsel lacked authority to consent; the order recorded that the parties had sought disposal on the compromise terms.
The allegation that the Advocate General had not appeared was raised only later, and the court record stated that the State was represented.
issues.conclusion: The writ court’s consent order was not invalid merely because the compromise was not separately signed by the parties. The requirements of Order XXIII Rule 3 CPC did not have to be mandatorily followed in the Article 226 proceedings, and the recorded account of what occurred in court could not be contradicted in the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 24 of the Andhra Pradesh Writ Proceedings Rules applies the CPC as far as possible, while Section 141 CPC excludes Article 226 proceedings from the expression “proceedings”; Order XXIII Rule 3 CPC therefore does not control the High Court’s power under Article 226 to dispose of a matter by consent. The court relied on Byram Pestonji Gariwala v. Union Bank of India for the authority of counsel to act for a client, and State of Maharashtra v. Ramdas Shrinivas Nayak for the principle that a court’s record of what occurred before it is conclusive unless corrected by that court.

predicates.article_226_proceeding: The matter is a proceeding before a court exercising constitutional writ jurisdiction.
predicates.consent_terms_recorded_by_court: The court records that the parties, through counsel, agreed to disposal on stated compromise terms.
predicates.counsel_authority_undisputed: The party does not establish that the counsel who consented lacked authority to act for it.

issues.definition: When a court exercising writ jurisdiction records the parties’ consent through counsel and counsel’s authority is undisputed, the consent order is not invalid solely because the parties did not separately sign a compromise.

issues.legal_issue: An appeal challenging an order made by consent is not maintainable where the order records the parties’ consent and the asserted grounds do not establish a basis to invalidate that consent.
material_facts: The writ petition was disposed of on terms recorded by the court as a compromise agreed to by counsel for both parties.
The appellants did not appeal that order at the time and later filed a writ appeal challenging it.

The allegation that the compromise had not been authorized or that the recorded consent was false was not made until late in the proceedings, and the court found no sufficient basis for disturbing the order.
issues.conclusion: The High Court correctly upheld the preliminary objection to the maintainability of the appeal against the consent order.
issues.legal_principle: The court upheld the objection based on Section 96(3) CPC, which bars an appeal from a decree passed with the consent of the parties, and found no established ground on the facts to undo the recorded consent. It also applied the principle in State of Maharashtra v. Ramdas Shrinivas Nayak that statements in a judgment recording what occurred in court cannot be contradicted on appeal.

predicates.appeal_challenges_consent_order: A party brings an appeal challenging an order that was made on the basis of recorded consent.
predicates.consent_recorded_by_court: The order records that the parties agreed to the disposition through their representatives.
predicates.no_proven_basis_to_set_consent_aside: The appellant does not establish that the recorded consent should be invalidated.

issues.definition: An appeal challenging a court-recorded consent order is not maintainable when the appellant establishes no basis for setting aside the consent.

issues.legal_issue: A finding on a matter essential to an earlier final decision binds the parties in later proceedings even if no formal issue was framed on that matter.
material_facts: In the earlier civil suit, the Endowments Commissioner pleaded that the gift deed gave only a general power of attorney, making the nature and effect of the deed material to the dispute.
The first appellate court and the High Court found that the land had been gifted absolutely, that the Government had no interest in it, and that the private temple did not make the land an endowment.
The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals from those decisions and stated that the findings had to be sustained.
The appellants later sought to reopen those findings, although they had become final and were necessary to resolve the earlier dispute.
issues.conclusion: The findings in the earlier litigation were binding and could not be reopened; the bar of res judicata applied despite the absence of a formally framed issue.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 CPC embodies res judicata. Under Sajjadanashin Sayed v. Musa Dadabhai Ummer, whether a matter was directly and substantially in issue depends on whether its decision was material and essential to the earlier judgment, assessed from the pleadings and decision rather than solely from the formal issues. The court also relied on Vithal Yeshwant Jathar v. Shikandarkhan Makhtumkhan Sardesai and Raj Laxmi Dasi v. Banamali Sen, and distinguished decisions concerning incidental findings or decisions made without jurisdiction.

predicates.later_proceeding_between_same_parties: A later proceeding concerns the same parties or persons claiming through them.
predicates.earlier_decision_final: An earlier court decision resolving the matter has become final.
predicates.disputed_finding_essential_to_earlier_de: The disputed finding was material and necessary to the earlier court’s decision, even if no formal issue was framed on it.

issues.definition: When parties return to court after a final decision, a finding essential to that decision cannot be relitigated even if it was not set out as a formal issue.

issues.legal_issue: Statutory provisions governing public charitable institutions and endowments do not apply to property found to be an absolute private gift unconnected with a public endowment.
material_facts: The final findings in the earlier litigation established that the land had been gifted absolutely to an individual and that the temple constructed on part of it was private.
The gift deed did not create an endowment, and the Government had no interest in the land.

The appellants relied on the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1987, including its provisions concerning administration and adjudication of endowment matters.
The fact that the premises had been used as a dharamshala for years was relied on as suggesting a public endowment.
issues.conclusion: The Act did not apply to the property, so the appellants’ reliance on its provisions did not undermine the consent order or the prior findings.
issues.legal_principle: Section 1(3) of the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1987 applies to public charitable institutions and endowments. The court relied on Deoki Nandan v. Murlidhar for the distinction between private and public trusts, and Kuldip Chand v. Advocate-General to hold that long use of property as a dharamshala, by itself, does not establish dedication to the public.

predicates.property_found_to_be_absolute_private_gi: The evidence and binding findings establish that the property was given absolutely to a private recipient.
predicates.temple_found_to_be_private: The place of worship on the property is found to be private rather than public.
predicates.no_public_endowment_established: The facts do not establish that the property was dedicated for the benefit of the public as a class.

issues.definition: Property found to be an absolute private gift associated with a private temple, without an established public dedication, falls outside rules for public endowments.
